steps.title: FROM TOKENS TO WORDS: ON THE INNER LEXICON OF LLMS

core_judgments: The idea of an inner lexicon is not new, as it follows implicitly from prior work on memorization of training data and explicitly from research on tokenization methods such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), which is extensively discussed in the paper.
Many of the findings in this work reproduce and analyze well-established concepts in this area.
The final experiment introducing a method for training-free vocabulary expansion appears to be a novel contribution, but it is only briefly explored and would benefit from deeper investigation.

The idea of an inner lexicon is not new, as it follows implicitly from prior work on memorization of training data and explicitly from research on tokenization methods such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), which is extensively discussed in the paper.
Many of the findings in this work reproduce and analyze well-established concepts in this area (subword tokenization and vocabulary learning).
The final experiment introducing a method for training-free vocabulary expansion appears to be a novel contribution, but it is only briefly explored and would benefit from deeper investigation.

conclusion: The paper’s central contribution is the claim that LLMs internally detokenize subword sequences into coherent whole-word representations, primarily in early–middle layers, and that these multi-token words form a latent internal lexicon. Very similar conclusions are already drawn in Feucht et al. (2024), who show that multi-token lexical items undergo an early-layer “detokenization/erasure” process and that multi-token sequences are recoverable from early hidden states, and in Lad et al. (2024), who likewise document early-layer integration of subtokens into whole-word/entity representations using logit-lens-style analyses. Relative to these, the present submission mainly offers alternative probes and interventions (controlled random splits, word/nonword contrasts, Patchscopes-based decoding, and more task-specific retrieval metrics), which refine and repackage the same core picture rather than substantially changing it. The more novel elements — explicit logit-lens reconstruction of original words, evidence that FFN layers retrieve full-word representations earlier than residual streams, and some finer-grained characterization of robustness and FFN causality — are secondary mechanistic details on top of an already-established phenomenon. Given that the core detokenization/latent-vocabulary mechanism is substantially anticipated by Feucht et al. (2024) and Lad et al. (2024), the overall novelty is not sufficient for a top-venue publication.
